Corruptly
cor-rupt'ly
adv. (in a corrupt manner; viciously; with depravity; contrary to purity)
From corrupt, Latin corrumpere, to break to pieces, to spoil, from con- and rumpere, to break. Corruption in the root sense is not filth added but soundness broken.

Biblical Definition

Twice the Authorized Version uses the adverb, and the two places show the sin at its two levels — the nation's and the penitent's. The first is the verdict on Jotham's reign: “And he did that which was right in the sight of the LORD, according to all that his father Uzziah did: howbeit he entered not into the temple of the LORD. And the people did yet corruptly” (2Ch 27:2). It is one of the saddest sentences in Chronicles. A genuinely good king, careful where his father had presumed, and the people go on corrupting anyway. A righteous magistrate cannot make a people holy; reformation from the throne reaches only so deep. The second is Nehemiah on his knees: “We have dealt very corruptly against thee, and have not kept the commandments, nor the statutes, nor the judgments, which thou commandedst thy servant Moses” (Neh 1:7). Note the pronoun. Nehemiah was in Persia, a boy or unborn when the walls fell, and he says we. That is covenantal confession, and it is the posture that actually precedes rebuilding. The root of the whole matter is stated at the flood: “God looked upon the earth, and, behold, it was corrupt; for all flesh had corrupted his way upon the earth” (Gen 6:12).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines corruptly as in a corrupt manner; with corruption; viciously; wickedly; by bribery.

expand to see more

CORRUPT'LY, adv.

In a corrupt manner; viciously; wickedly; without integrity.

We have dealt very corruptly against thee. Neh. 1.

By bribes; by means of corruption; as a judge who decides corruptly.

From the Latin corrumpere, to break in pieces, to spoil; con and rumpo, to break.

Key Scripture

2 Chronicles 27:2 — "And he did that which was right in the sight of the LORD, according to all that his father Uzziah did: howbeit he entered not into the temple of the LORD. And the people did yet corruptly."

Nehemiah 1:7 — "We have dealt very corruptly against thee, and have not kept the commandments, nor the statutes, nor the judgments, which thou commandedst thy servant Moses."

Genesis 6:12 — "And God looked upon the earth, and, behold, it was corrupt; for all flesh had corrupted his way upon the earth."

Proverbs 17:15 — "He that justifieth the wicked, and he that condemneth the just, even they both are abomination to the LORD."

Modern Corruption

Corruption is treated as a problem of systems to be re-engineered rather than of hearts to be renewed, and so reform never reaches the thing that is broken.

expand to see more

2 Chronicles 27:2 is the permanent rebuke to political messianism in every century. Jotham did right; he was more careful than his father; and the people did yet corruptly. Scripture records good administration and continued corruption in the same verse without treating it as a contradiction, because the throne governs conduct and cannot govern the heart. Christians who have staked everything on capturing an office, and Christians who despair because the office was lost, are both reading this verse as though it could not be true. The civil magistrate is a real ordinance of God with a real sphere; it has never been a means of grace.

Nehemiah 1:7 supplies what the age finds hardest — a confession in the first person plural by a man who could plausibly have used the third. Modern discourse about corruption is almost entirely accusatory: it is always they who have dealt corruptly, and the speaker's role is diagnosis. Nehemiah names himself and his father's house before he asks for anything, and it is from that posture that the walls actually go up. Genesis 6:12 explains why the plural is honest: all flesh had corrupted his way, and the Reformed doctrine of original sin is simply this verse read without flinching.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew shachath (H7843), to spoil, ruin, corrupt; chabal (H2254), to act corruptly, to bind in pledge; Latin corrumpere, to break in pieces.

expand to see more

Hebrew chabol chabalnu (H2254) — corrupting we have corrupted; Nehemiah 1:7, the doubled verb the Authorized Version renders very corruptly.

Hebrew shachath (H7843) — to spoil, to ruin, to destroy; Genesis 6:12, all flesh had corrupted its way.

Hebrew mashchith (H4889) — a ruin, corruption; the noun from the same root, used of the destroyer.

Greek phtheiro (G5351) — to corrupt, to spoil; 1 Corinthians 15:33, evil communications corrupt good manners.

Latin corrumpere, from con- and rumpere — to break to pieces; corruption is soundness broken, not filth added.

Usage

"“And the people did yet corruptly” — under a good king, and the verse says both."

"“We have dealt very corruptly against thee” — the pronoun is the repentance."

"“All flesh had corrupted his way” — original sin stated as a survey of the earth."
